lessons.question: Your app gets an HTTP success back from a model API. Can it safely use the answer straight away?
options: Yes, success means the model answered correctly
Not yet, because completion and content still need checking
Only if the response arrived quickly
lessons.explanation: HTTP success only says the transport worked. The response may still be incomplete, a refusal, or well-formed but wrong, so each layer needs its own check.

lessons.after: For ticket triage, define four fields:
lessons.prompt: Does each piece of triage output follow the field rules?

items.text: needs_review is the string 'yes'
category is scheduling
category is urgent
needs_review is the Boolean true
reason quotes what the customer asked for
reason claims a past refund the ticket never mentions

lessons.explanation: Categories come from a fixed list, the review flag must be a real Boolean, and the reason must cite the request rather than invent facts.

lessons.prompt: Which kind of check would catch each problem?

items.text: The reason field is missing entirely
Category is shipping, which is not an allowed value
An unknown category was not sent to review
A refund is recorded as already approved
The reason misreads what the customer wanted
A reviewer says this ticket needed review but the flag says no

lessons.explanation: Schema checks shape and allowed values, business checks enforce relationships and rules, and semantic evaluation asks whether the decision is actually right.

lessons.after: All four fields have the right types.
lessons.prompt: T09 passed every type check. What rule could have stopped this decision before it reached staff?
lessons.answer: A business rule for mixed intent: when a ticket asks about more than one thing, such as an invoice and a visit change, set needs_review to true. The reference policy sends mixed intent to review, whatever the parser says.

lessons.question: A model call fails. What is the smartest first move?
options: Work out what kind of failure it is
Save the full raw request permanently
lessons.explanation: Different failures need different responses. Retrying a malformed request or a wrong credential unchanged just wastes time without fixing anything.

lessons.question: A call that creates a booking times out, and you cannot tell whether it went through. What is the risk of simply resending?
options: It may create a duplicate booking
The model will forget the ticket
lessons.explanation: A side-effecting action may already have happened. Without idempotency or reconciliation on the receiving side, a retry can repeat it.

lessons.after: Record request ID, case ID, prompt version
lessons.prompt: You are designing the log for each model call. Record it, or keep it out?

items.text: Request ID
Prompt version
Token usage, when exposed
The API key used for the call
Unneeded personal details from the ticket
Why the item went to review

lessons.explanation: Logs should let you trace and explain each call. Credentials and unnecessary personal content create risk without helping diagnosis.

lessons.after: Cost per attempted call can make a poor
lessons.question: Using illustrative prices, a call uses 1,000 input tokens at AUD 0.002 per thousand and 500 output tokens at AUD 0.008 per thousand. What is its estimated cost?
lessons.explanation: Input is 1 × 0.002 = 0.002 and output is 0.5 × 0.008 = 0.004, giving 0.006. Input and output are priced separately, so estimate each and add them.

lessons.prompt: Before you read on: in what order would you test a structured triage step?
steps: Inspect the schema and the validator
Validate a known good example response
Break a copy and confirm it is rejected with a reason
Send one fictional ticket to a live model
Evaluate at least twenty cases and record the results
lessons.explanation: Start offline so you know the checks work, prove that bad output is rejected, then spend live calls, and finally measure across a set rather than a few examples.

lessons.after: Missing customer information is not a licence
lessons.question: A ticket arrives with no customer ID. The model returns a neatly formatted ID anyway. What should happen?
options: Accept it, because the format is valid
Ask the model to rate its confidence
Treat it as invented and route it for review
lessons.explanation: A well-shaped value is not evidence it is true. Missing information should produce a visible review or error outcome, never a made-up ID.

lessons.prompt: In your write-up, which validations run automatically and which need a person?

items.text: Category is one of the four allowed values
needs_review is a Boolean
Unknown categories are routed to review
Resolving an item flagged for review
Judging whether a reason fairly reflects the request

lessons.explanation: Shape and rule checks are mechanical, so code can enforce them. Deciding what an ambiguous request really means still needs a responsible person.
